source_refs.note: Topic 32.3.2 with the Did You Know box (PDF 235-236); the receptor diagram is original. The book's grouping of fentanyl as an illegal opiate is clarified in a warning.

blocks.text: Opiates are a class of drugs that come from the opium poppy plant. They are powerful painkillers but also cause addiction. The book lists morphine, codeine, oxycodone and hydrocodone as legal drugs, and heroin and fentanyl among illegal ones.

blocks.title: Opiates and opioids
blocks.text: Strictly, opiates are the natural compounds from the poppy (morphine, codeine). Oxycodone, hydrocodone and heroin are made from them, and fentanyl is fully synthetic; together they are called opioids. Fentanyl is also a legal prescription medicine (for example in anaesthesia), though it is made and sold illegally as well.

blocks.title: Opioid receptors
blocks.text: The human brain makes its own painkillers called endorphins, which bind to opioid receptors in the central nervous system (CNS). Opiates 'hijack' this natural system: they relieve pain but are also highly addictive.

items: Mu receptors are in the brain and spinal cord. They are the main target of most opioids such as morphine and are responsible for pain relief, but activating them can also cause respiratory depression (slowed breathing) and intense euphoria.
Kappa receptors are involved in spinal pain relief and sedation, but are less linked to euphoria.
Delta receptors play a vital role in emotional response and mood regulation.

blocks.text: Opiates work by binding to special proteins in the brain and spinal cord called opioid receptors, like a key (the opiate) in a lock (the receptor). When an opiate binds, it blocks pain signals from reaching the brain, so the person feels less pain. In fact, binding closes calcium channels and opens potassium channels. This hyperpolarises the neuron, making it much harder for the cell to send the pain signal. Opiates also trigger the release of a large amount of dopamine in the brain's reward centre, which gives a sense of relief and well-being.

blocks.alt: Left: a nerve-cell membrane drawn as a horizontal band. On it a receptor shaped like a lock holds an opiate shaped like a key. Beside it a calcium channel is shown closed and a potassium channel open, with an arrow showing K+ flowing out. Text: the neuron becomes hyperpolarised so the pain signal is hard to send; dopamine in the reward centre gives relief and well-being. Right: three cards for the mu, kappa and delta receptors and their roles; endorphins are the body's own painkillers.
blocks.caption: Opiates and opioid receptors (original diagram for topic 32.3.2).
blocks.long_description: The opiate fits the receptor as a key fits a lock. The changes in the calcium and potassium channels quieten the nerve cell, which is why pain is felt less; the dopamine release is linked to addiction.

blocks.text: Opioids are used to relieve acute pain (sudden, short-term pain) and to manage the severe pain associated with cancer. Codeine is used in cough syrups because it suppresses the cough reflex. Opioids also bind to receptors in the gastrointestinal tract, slowing digestion, so they can relieve diarrhoea.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Before it became a street drug, heroin (diacetylmorphine) was a trademarked medicine sold by Bayer as a 'non-addictive' alternative to morphine and as a cough suppressant for children. Its potency is roughly five times that of morphine and it crosses the blood-brain barrier faster, creating a 'rush' that led to a global addiction epidemic.

blocks.prompt: Which opioid receptor is the main target of morphine, and what side effects can its activation cause?
blocks.explanation: The mu receptor; besides pain relief, it can cause respiratory depression and intense euphoria.

items: Opiates bind opioid receptors (key and lock), like the body's endorphins.
Ca2+ channels close, K+ channels open: neuron hyperpolarised, pain signal blocked.
Mu, kappa, delta receptors; uses: pain, cough, diarrhoea; addictive.
